title: Tree diagrams
examples: When do I use a tree diagram?
What is the difference between with and without replacement?
How do I calculate the final probability from the branches?

explain.say: Today we learn about tree diagrams for probability. These help us see all the possible outcomes. We will look at two main ways things can happen.

draw.text: Tree Diagrams: With and Without Replacement

explain.say: First, let us look at events with replacement. This means after the first pick, you put the item back. The chances stay exactly the same for the second pick.
For example, you pick a coin, note the result, and put it back. Then you pick it again. The probability of heads is always one half.
Next, we look at events without replacement. Here, you keep the first item out. This changes the total number of items for the second pick.
Consider picking two marbles without putting the first one back. If you take a red marble first, there are fewer red marbles left.

faq.q: When should I use a tree diagram?
faq.a: You use a tree diagram when you have two or more events happening one after the other. It helps you map out every possible sequence of results.
asks: How many steps are needed for a tree diagram?
Do I always need a tree diagram for probability?

faq.a: It means that after you record the result of the first event, you put the item back into the group. This keeps the probabilities unchanged.
asks: Does the total number change if it is with replacement?
Is the probability the same every time?

faq.a: It means you keep the first item you picked out. This reduces the total number of items and sometimes the number of specific items.
asks: Does the second pick have fewer options?
How do I adjust the numbers for the second pick?

faq.q: How do I find the final probability?
faq.a: To find the probability of a whole path, you multiply the probabilities along each branch. You then add up the probabilities of all the paths you are interested in.
asks: Do I add or multiply the probabilities?
What do I do with the numbers on the branches?

faq.q: If I pick two blue marbles, how do I calculate that?
faq.a: You must build a tree diagram showing the first blue pick and then the second blue pick. You multiply the probabilities for that specific path.
asks: What if I want the probability of blue then red?
Do I calculate it for each color separately?

facts: The probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes.
When events are independent, the probability of both happening is the product of their individual probabilities.
Without replacement, the total number of items decreases by one for the second event.
A tree diagram shows all possible outcomes in sequence.

quiz.say: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. You pick one, do not replace it, and then pick a second marble. What is the probability of picking two blue marbles?
quiz.why: The first probability is two divided by five. The second is one divided by four, so you multiply them: two fifths times one fourth equals two twentieths, which simplifies to one fifteenth.

wrong.1: This is wrong because you incorrectly added the probabilities instead of multiplying them.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you treated the events as if the first marble was replaced.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you multiplied the initial probabilities without accounting for the change in the second draw.

quiz.say: A box contains 4 black and 6 white cards. You draw one card, keep it out, and then draw a second card. What is the probability of drawing a black card first, and then a white card second?
quiz.why: The first draw is four over ten. The second draw is six over nine. Multiplying these gives twenty-four over ninety, which simplifies to two fifteenths.

wrong.1: This is wrong because you incorrectly used the original total of ten for both draws.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you only considered the probability of the first draw.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you only considered the probability of the second draw.
